sections.h: "In the hand of his own choice" (Sirach 15:11-20)
sections.b: Sirach gives the clearest statement of human freedom outside the 66 books. Its student must not say, "The Lord is the reason I turned away" (Sirach 15:11), because God "made the human being at the start / and left him in the hand of his own choice" (Sirach 15:14). Fire and water, life and death lie before each person (Sirach 15:16-17), in the words of Deuteronomy 30:15-19. The Hebrew of Cairo Genizah manuscript A has yetser, "inclination," where the Greek has "choice," the first step toward the rabbis' teaching of the good and evil inclinations (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5; Kiddushin 30b). The passage became a battleground: Augustine quoted it against those who blame God for their sins; Erasmus brought it first against Luther, who replied that it speaks of rule over the creatures; Calvin read it of humanity as first made; the Catholic Catechism cites it for human freedom (1730). See the card on Sirach 15.

common: Sirach 15:14 is the classic text in the Old Testament books of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles for human free choice.
uncommon: Luther read the "counsel" in which God left humanity, in Sirach 15:14, as humanity's rule over the lower creatures, not freedom toward God.

sections.b: Sirach 13 is a clear-eyed lesson on living near the rich. Partnership with the powerful is a clay pot against a metal cauldron (Sirach 13:2); the rich man uses you, shames you with his dinners and laughs at you (Sirach 13:4-7); when he slips, all help him, and when the poor man speaks sense no one listens (Sirach 13:21-23). Yet "wealth is good if there is no sin in it" (Sirach 13:24). Chapter 14 attacks the opposite fault, the miser who will not even spend on himself (Sirach 14:3-10), and urges using one's goods while alive, for oneself, for friends and for God (Sirach 14:11-16). Chapter 18 adds a warning against running up debts for banquets (Sirach 18:32-33), in the words Deuteronomy uses for the glutton (Deuteronomy 21:20).
sections.refs: Sirach 13:1-26; Sirach 14:3-19; Sirach 18:32-33; Proverbs 19:4; Ecclesiastes 4:8; Luke 12:16-21

sections.b: Ben Sira describes the poor through the eyes of the powerful: "Wild donkeys in the desert are what lions hunt; / so the poor are pasture for the rich" (Sirach 13:19), and "a poor man is abhorrent to the rich" (Sirach 13:20). He records, without softening, how a poor man's good sense is ignored (Sirach 13:22-23), as Ecclesiastes 9:16 does. The picture matches the prophets' charge against those who "grind the faces of the poor" (Isaiah 3:15) and James's against favoritism (James 2:1-7).

Ben Sira pictures the student as a lover of Wisdom: he tracks her, lies in wait at her doors, peers through her windows, camps by her walls and sets his children in her shade (Sirach 14:20-27). She comes out to meet him "like a mother," welcomes him like the wife of his youth, and feeds him "bread of understanding" (Sirach 15:2-3). The way to her is the fear of the Lord and a firm hold on the law (Sirach 15:1). The poem draws on Proverbs 8:34 and 9:5 and prepares for Wisdom's own speech in Sirach 24.
sections.refs: Sirach 14:20-15:10; Proverbs 8:34; Proverbs 9:5; Song of Songs 2:9; Wisdom of Solomon 8:2; John 6:35

sections.h: No praise and no luxury in Hades (Sirach 14 and 17)
sections.b: Ben Sira holds the older biblical view of the dead. "The covenant of Hades" is the fixed rule that all must die (Sirach 14:12, 17); "no one goes looking for luxury in Hades" (Sirach 14:16); and "In Hades, who will praise the Most High / instead of the living, who give him thanks?" (Sirach 17:27). He agrees with Psalm 6:5, Psalm 115:17 and Isaiah 38:18-19 and speaks of no resurrection. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, which include Sirach, also include 2 Maccabees with its hope that "the King of the world will raise us" (2 Maccabees 7:9).
sections.refs: Sirach 14:12-19; Sirach 17:27-28; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 115:17; Isaiah 38:18-19; 2 Maccabees 7:9

sections.h: Almsgiving kept like a seal ring (Sirach 16:14; 17:22)
sections.b: Sirach says the Lord "will make room for every gift of alms" (Sirach 16:14), where the Hebrew has "everyone who does tsedaqah has a reward," and that "a man's alms are with him like a seal ring" (Sirach 17:22): God keeps it safe. The Latin of 16:14 speaks of "the merit of his works." Ben Sira also teaches how to give: without blame or hurtful words, since "a word is worth more than a gift" (Sirach 18:15-17). Compare 2 Corinthians 9:7 and Matthew 6:2-4, and the card at Tobit 4.
sections.refs: Sirach 16:14; Sirach 17:22; Sirach 18:15-18; Tobit 4:7-11; Matthew 6:2-4; 2 Corinthians 9:7

sections.b: After warning that God will repay every sin, Ben Sira says that "for those who repent he has opened a road back" (Sirach 17:24), and calls: "Turn back to the Lord and leave your sins behind" (Sirach 17:25). His reason is urgent: only the living can praise God (Sirach 17:27-28). His call takes up the prophets' (Hosea 14:1-2; Joel 2:12-13; Zechariah 1:3), and his confidence in the atonement God gives "those who turn back to him" (Sirach 17:29) matches 2 Peter 3:9.
sections.refs: Sirach 17:24-29; Sirach 18:21; Hosea 14:1-2; Joel 2:12-13; Zechariah 1:3; 2 Peter 3:9

sections.b: Ben Sira holds mercy and anger together: "mercy and anger are both with him" (Sirach 16:11), echoing Exodus 34:6-7. But his hymn of chapter 18 leans toward mercy: because human life is so short, "the Lord bears with them a long time / and pours his mercy out on them" (Sirach 18:11), and "the Lord's mercy reaches all flesh," like a shepherd with his flock (Sirach 18:13). Jonah 4:11 and Wisdom of Solomon 11:23 make the same point.
sections.refs: Sirach 16:11-12; Sirach 17:29; Sirach 18:11-14; Exodus 34:6-7; Jonah 4:11; Wisdom of Solomon 11:23

sections.b: Sirach 17 retells Genesis 1-2: God made humans from earth, gave them numbered days and rule over the creatures, "clothed them with strength fit for them / and made them in his image" (Sirach 17:3). The list that follows, choice, tongue, eyes, ears, a heart to think, knowledge and the knowledge of good and evil (Sirach 17:6-7), shows how Ben Sira understood the image: the gifts of reason and responsible freedom, joined to rule over the world.

"For each nation he appointed a ruler, / but Israel is the Lord's share" (Sirach 17:17) echoes Deuteronomy 32:8-9, whose Septuagint reads "according to the number of the angels of God" and calls Israel meris Kyriou, "the Lord's portion." The "ruler" may be an angelic prince like those of Daniel 10:13, 20, or the nation's king (compare Sirach 10:4). Either way Israel has God himself as its ruler.

Sirach lists among God's past judgments "the giants of long ago, / who broke away from him in their strength" (Sirach 16:7). The Greek uses the Septuagint's word for the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4, gigantes; the Hebrew of manuscript A has "the princes of old." Wisdom of Solomon 14:6, 3 Maccabees 2:4 and Baruch 3:26-28 make the giants examples of pride punished, and 1 Enoch 6-7 tells their fuller story.
sections.refs: Sirach 16:7; Genesis 6:4; Wisdom of Solomon 14:6; 3 Maccabees 2:4; Baruch 3:26-28; 1 Enoch 7:2

sections.b: Ben Sira does not name Sodom; he says God "did not spare the place where Lot lived as a stranger, / the people he abhorred because of their pride" (Sirach 16:8). Pride is also Ezekiel's charge against Sodom (Ezekiel 16:49-50) and 3 Maccabees' ("The Sodomites practiced arrogance," 3 Maccabees 2:5).

sections.h: Pharaoh in the longer text of Sirach (Sirach 16:15)
sections.b: A line missing from Codex Vaticanus but found in the Hebrew of manuscript A and in later Greek copies says, "The Lord hardened Pharaoh so that he would not know him, / so that his works would become known to the world under heaven" (Sirach 16:15). It stands only a chapter after Ben Sira's denial that God makes anyone sin (Sirach 15:11-20), and like Exodus and Romans 9:17-18 it holds God's rule and human guilt together.

Ben Sira quotes God's warning in Eden, "You will die, yes die," as "the covenant of ages past" that binds all flesh (Sirach 14:17; Genesis 2:17), but in his retelling of creation he says God himself "pointed out to them what is good and what is evil" (Sirach 17:7), and he tells no story of a fall there. Death is part of the created order (Sirach 17:1-2). Elsewhere he speaks of where sin began, in the much-debated Sirach 25:24. The longer Greek of Sirach 17:16 adds a darker line: "Every person from youth up is bent on evil."
sections.refs: Sirach 14:17; Sirach 17:1-7; Sirach 17:16; Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:5; Genesis 8:21; Romans 5:12

sections.b: "Do not let anything keep you from paying a vow when it is due, / and do not wait until death to be justified" (Sirach 18:22), and "Get yourself ready before you make a vow" (Sirach 18:23), where the Hebrew says "prepare your vow." Ben Sira repeats Deuteronomy 23:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5: a careless vow puts the Lord to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16). The Latin of 18:22 reads instead "Let nothing hinder thee from praying always."

The Greek of Sirach 18:1 says the eternal God "created all things together" (koinē, "in common, all alike"). The Latin rendered it simul, "at the same time," and Augustine quoted the line ("creavit omnia simul") in The Literal Meaning of Genesis (6.3.4; 6.6.11) in his argument that God made all things at once, so that the six days are not ordinary stretches of time. The Greek itself stresses that God made everything, not when.

The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Kamma 92b) traces a proverb through "the Torah ... the Prophets, and ... the Writings," and for the Writings quotes, "Every bird nests with its kind, and a human being with one like him," a form of Sirach 13:15-16. Elsewhere the Talmud records Rav Yosef forbidding the reading of Ben Sira (Sanhedrin 100b). The rabbis did not count the book as Scripture, yet its sayings were sometimes cited as if they stood among the Writings.

Sirach 16 lists past judgments, the gathering of sinners burned, the giants, Sodom, the Canaanites and the wilderness generation (Sirach 16:6-10), to prove that "he will judge a man according to his works" (Sirach 16:12, 14), the language of Psalm 62:12 and Romans 2:6. Chapter 17 adds that God sees all and "will rise and repay them" (Sirach 17:23), while leaving "a road back" for the repentant (Sirach 17:24). Ben Sira expects the repayment within this life or at death (Sirach 18:24).
sections.refs: Sirach 16:6-14; Sirach 17:19-24; Sirach 18:24; Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; 2 Peter 2:4-6

sections.b: Ben Sira answers the sinner who thinks he is lost in the crowd: "what is my one soul in a creation too great to measure?" (Sirach 16:17). Heaven and earth shake when God comes (Sirach 16:18-19), and "his eyes stay fixed on their ways without a break" (Sirach 17:19). Compare Psalm 139:7-12 and Jeremiah 23:24.
